title: Until Dawn 2's sun-kissed horror gets a PS5 release date - and the studio behind last year's brilliant Dispatch is involved
author: Matt Wales
content:
Following its big Summer Game Fest unveiling earlier this year, Until Dawn 2 has been given a release date as part of Sony's latest State of Play showcase. And it's not far away at all, launching for PS5 in the suitably dark depths of winter: arriving 28th January next year.
As we learned previously, some big changes are afoot in Until Dawn 2. For starters, the snow-covered alpine resort setting of the first game is making way for sun-kissed tropical climes, where a successful crew of TV ghosthunters (the Dead True) is about to embark on its latest assignment.
"After an investigation at Blackwood Sanitorium takes a chilling turn," Sony explains in its release date announcement, "an encounter with supernatural survivor Yoona leads them to Akishima Island, a remote paradise abandoned for decades and hiding secrets far older than any of them imagined."
![Cover image for YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/-wjhso38sAY/hqdefault.jpg) Until Dawn 2 - Choice & Consequence Pre-Order Trailer | PS5 Games
New characters does, of course, mean a new cast - but, notably, one familiar face is returning: Peter Stormare, who played Until Dawn 1's memorably unhinged psychiatrist Dr. Hill, is back and will presumably be fulfilling a similar role. Quite how that'll work in story terms, however - given some of the things we learn in the original game - Sony hasn't yet said.
Until Dawn 2 - which follows 2024's Until Dawn 1 remake - is being developed by Sony's Liverpool-based Firesprite Games, rather than original studio Supermassive. Interestingly, though, it's now been confirmed AdHoc Studio - the team behind last year's superb Dispatch - is involved in a narrative capacity.
"So you can expect a deeply layered story packed with rich characters, razor-sharp dialogue, fraught relationships, tough decisions, and yes... more than a few gruesome deaths," Firesprite creative director Stu Tilley writes. "Every choice, every interaction can ripple with dramatic consequences."
Alongside the standard edition of Until Dawn 2, Sony has also unveiled a Deluxe Digital Edition also releasing on 28th January. This adds the Y2K Neon Vibes Pack featuring new outfits for each of the core cast, plus the Diorama of Death. "Relive every grisly demise with vignettes exploring unique angles of each fatal outcome," explains Sony. "Can you unlock every scene?". And if you choose to pre-order starting 10th September, there are some Dr. Hill-themed bits to be gained: the Until Dawn classic outfit, the Akishima Island holiday outfit, and some Dr. Hill collector's bobbleheads to discover in-game.
And while we're on the subject of Until Dawn, Eurogamer celebrated the original's 10th anniversary last year by chatting with the game's creator, Will Byles, about its enormously eventful development. We discussed the challenges the studio faced, the lengths it went to to break new ground, and how Sony reportedly attempted to bury the game on release. It's a fascinating story and well worth a read!
summary: Sony has announced that Until Dawn 2 will release for the PS5 on January 28 next year. Moving away from the original's snow-covered setting, the sequel takes place on Akishima Island and follows a crew of TV ghosthunters. Developed by Firesprite Games with narrative involvement from AdHoc Studio, the game features a new cast alongside returning actor Peter Stormare.
key_points: Until Dawn 2 launches exclusively for PS5 on January 28 next year.
The setting shifts from an alpine resort to the tropical Akishima Island.
Peter Stormare returns to reprise his role, alongside a new cast of characters.
The game is developed by Firesprite Games with narrative contribution from AdHoc Studio.
A Deluxe Digital Edition and pre-order bonuses have been announced by Sony.

title: NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs Arrive Next Month In Two "N1X" SoC Configs, One With a 20 Core CPU, 6144 Core GPU & Up To 128 GB Memory, Other With 18 Core CPU, 5120 Core GPU & Up To 32 GB Memory
author: Hassan Mujtaba
content:
NVIDIA's RTX Spark PCs are officially launching in October, powered by the N1X SoC, to deliver game-changing performance & efficiency.
NVIDIA Is Ready To Launch Its Game-Changing RTX Spark PCs In October, Top N1X Designs Hit Shelves First
The RTX Spark is a PC platform first, made for consumers, and designed to run games, content creation, and AI tasks. It's an all-in-one solution, backed by the first-generation N-series chip, called N1X.
Today at IFA, NVIDIA is finally announcing a launch date for its first full-fledged client PC platform. The NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs will be hitting shelves next month in October, and that is exciting as we see NVIDIA's arrival in a space where they had only offered GPUs prior to this day. With RTX Spark "N1X", they will offer an SoC that combines an Arm CPU, a Blackwell RTX GPU, lots of memory, and much more.
![Lenovo and Acer announce new RTX Spark designs showcasing the Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 laptop and the Acer SFF RTX Spark desktop.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/NVIDIA-RTX-Spark-_-IFA-_2.jpg)
NVIDIA confirms that its OEMs will start commence RTX Spark shipments in October. The OEM list includes Acer, ASUS, Dell, Gigabyte, HP, MSI, Lenovo, and even Microsoft. NVIDIA told us that their target is to make sure that RTX Spark PCs are available in as many regions as possible at launch, but the final availability will vary across OEMs. Some OEMs will start with limited regions while the rest are going to go global.
N1X Comes In Two Flavors
In addition to the launch announcement, NVIDIA is also disclosing the first "official" specifications of the RTX Spark N1X chip. The N1X will be available in two configurations, and both will arrive in October.
![The 'RTX Spark N1X' image showcases specs for two configurations with Blackwell RTX GPUs, Grace CPUs, and unified memory options, set to arrive in October, featuring brands like ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and others.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/NVIDIA-RTX-Spark-_-IFA-_1-scaled.jpg)
The first configuration of the N1X will feature a 20-Core Grace CPU, a 6144-core Blackwell RTX GPU, unified memory configurations starting at 24 GB and going all the way up to 128 GB, and lots of IO capabilities. The top N1X configuration will be available in both laptops and compact desktop PCs at launch.
The second configuration of the N1X SoC will feature an 18-core Grace CPU, a 5120-core Blackwell RTX GPU, unified memory configurations starting at 24 GB and going up to 32 GB. This config will only be available on laptops at launch, but compact PC designs are expected later on.
The top configuration matches the GPU core count of the RTX 5070, while the second config has more CUDA cores than the RTX 5060 Ti. Now we don't expect these to match desktop or even the laptop configurations due to power and thermal constraints, but these will be able to offer really good gaming performance, putting them at the top of the iGPU rankings.
We have already seen some benchmarks of the 20- and 18-core Grace CPUs, which are really good in Geekbench. As for the GPU, we have only seen a few demos during our hands-on time at IFA and earlier, at Computex.
![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-mobile.png) 
![](https://cdn.wccftech.com/files/placeholder-desktop.png) 
RTX Spark Expectations
NVIDIA claims that the RTX Spark PCs will offer 100 FPS 1440p Gaming with various RT and DLSS innovations. These laptops will also support the latest DLSS updates such as DLSS 5 and DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction, along with MFG support up to 6x. NVIDIA has also announced various game developer and game publisher partnerships for RTX Spark at Gamescom, and we expect this to be the first fully performant "WoA" gaming solution on the market.
On the Content creation side, RTX Spark PC solutions will render 90GB 3D Scenes with OptiX & RT, while hardware-accelerated 4:2:2 video will ensure a rich creator experience.
![A laptop on a stand shows a system monitoring app with a 'CPU' usage graph, next to an external monitor displaying code.](https://cdn.wccftech.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/20260601_200112-1-scaled-1.jpg)
RTX Spark PCs will also feature the full NVIDIA AI stack, enabling up to 120B parameter agents with 1M context lengths. The Windows Agent Framework and optimizations in terms of Unified Memory will also ensure that the platform will be backed by proper support.
These PCs will come in designs as thin as 14mm and are said to offer all-day battery life. In our hands-on with various OEM designs, we got to see some super sleek and stylish laptops alongside Mini PCs.
Prices remain undisclosed, but considering the various memory tiers and the two N1X configs, we will see a wide spectrum of price options across various designs.
Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.
summary: NVIDIA is officially launching its RTX Spark PCs in October, powered by the new N1X system-on-chip that combines an Arm CPU and a Blackwell RTX GPU. The platform is designed for gaming, content creation, and AI tasks, and will be offered by various major OEMs in laptops and compact desktops. Two N1X configurations will be available at launch, featuring different core counts and unified memory options.
key_points: NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs launch in October with the N1X SoC, marking NVIDIA's entry into the client PC platform space.
The first N1X configuration includes a 20-core Grace CPU, a 6144-core Blackwell RTX GPU, and up to 128 GB of unified memory for laptops and compact desktops.
The second N1X configuration features an 18-core Grace CPU, a 5120-core Blackwell RTX GPU, and up to 32 GB of unified memory, available initially in laptops.
Major OEMs including Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and Microsoft will offer the new RTX Spark devices, with regional availability varying at launch.

title: Upgrade paths: Should Pixel 9 owners upgrade to Pixel 11? [Video]
author: Damien Wilde
content:
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Entire-Pixel-9-and-Pixel-11-family.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600) 
We’ve seen a lot of people ask if making the jump from the Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 is even worth it. The answer isn’t totally simple, but we’ll try our best to answer it here.
Table of contents
Your 24-month cell plan might be coming to an end, so it’s timely to talk about this switch now, and we’ll do our best to help you decide which phone is right, which phone is wrong, and ultimately whether an upgrade is worthwhile.
An unchanged design
Let’s get the obvious out of the way at the start: the Pixel 9 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro are very, very similar. You could be forgiven for thinking they are the same. For anyone with a non-Pro phone, you’ll see more pronounced changes, but for all intents and purposes, the designs are almost identical across the entire device lineup.
Let’s get into the actual improvements. No matter what Pixel 9 phone you have, all Pixel 11 displays are better. Maybe not drastically so, but you get a jump up in maximum brightness of around 10% on the Pixel 9 to 11. The Pros get a 20% brightness jump at peak. This is something you probably would notice, but still not a major change. All the screens are well tuned, there’s no bezel reduction, just the same great experience, but brighter.
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-9-Pro-and-Pixel-11-Pro-top-down.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-11-Pro-XL-and-9-Pro-XL-camera-side-profile.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-9-Pro-XL-and-11-Pro-XL-in-shot.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
We know the design is the same, the core frame dimensions are identical, the same height, width, and thickness. The only visible change is in the camera bar shape and size. You can’t use your old cases on the new phone, so that is an annoyance. The Pixel 9 and 11 are within 1g, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL are almost 10 grams heavier than the 9 Pro and Pro XL.
That could be due to the marginal battery size increases and maybe even the addition of Pixelsnap magnets, but it’s likely some internal changes that add a little extra mass, and better thermals too. Pixelsnap is great for connectivity, but a good case can mimic it pretty closely on the Pixel 9.
Similar software experience
One of the key differences between the Pixel 9 and Pixel 11 is Gemini Intelligence. It’s emblazoned all over the latest phone and adds some functionality that likely won’t come to the older devices unless Google has a change of heart.
You need to figure out if you care enough about some of the AI tools like App Automation, Rambler, the enhanced Proactive Assistant responses and replies for messaging, plus some of the other enhancements that the Pixel 10 added last year.
Some of this is merely fluff. Some are great features. Do they drastically improve your life? That remains to be seen.
Even the move from Tensor G4 up to the G6 chip might not be a big enough leap for lots of people. Neither is an amazing performance beast, but they’re competent chips that handle most things you’ll throw at either phone.
Faster storage is arguably a bigger ingredient in the equation because apps will load faster, and you also get the benefit of a 256GB base model now. It was a long-overdue quality of life change that will make a bigger difference in the long term.
Frustratingly, getting less RAM on the Pixel 11 Pro or Pro XL versus the Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL feels like a slap in the face. It’s not necessarily noticeable right now, save that you can have more apps in memory. Some of the RAM is wired for AI task control, so you’ll lose out here unless you pay more to get 16GB RAM.
The fact is, though, that the performance gap is not exactly a chasm, and Android 17 is identical here. Unless Google specifies otherwise, you’ll get all the same updates in the future too.
Quality cameras continue to impress
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-11-camera-with-Pixel-9-in-shot.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-9-and-Pixel-11-camera-UIs.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-11-Pro-XL-and-9-Pro-XL-cameras-compared.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Close-up-Pixel-11-Pro-and-Pixel-11-cameras.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=800)
If you want a telephoto lens and have the Pixel 9, then yes, you might want to upgrade. The digital zoom is not as good on the base 9. It’s capped and isn’t going to get close to the action.
The other lenses are fairly similar, but know that the main sensor is slightly larger on the Pixel 11. With the default settings, it’s a toss-up.
Camera Looks are where we get some notable improvements. These are sensor-level filters that you can customize to tune your Pixel 11 camera output. No Pixel 9 will get these tools. It’s arguably the biggest change on a Pixel camera since the addition of a triple camera setup.
If you have a Pro phone, there is a better telephoto lens that lets you zoom up to 120X. Video modes get some upgrades, AI-powered Magic Capture, plus a new Creator Mode is here too.
Like basically every other head-to-head comparison, the camera improvements are more about refinement than redefining, which makes a Pixel camera so reliable.
I don’t think someone would be disappointed at what has changed, maybe underwhelmed given the two-year leap. The reality is that a Pixel camera has mostly been about consistency, which hasn’t changed.
Is now the time to upgrade from the Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11?
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/09/Pixel-9-Pro-XL-and-11-Pro-XL-wide.jpg?quality=82&strip=all)
About upgrading: 9to5Google often gives specific product recommendations. Sometimes, we may suggest not upgrading, due to various reasons including, but not limited to: increased device cost, negligible performance gains, or environmental impact. Whether to upgrade is always your call, but our aim is to help you make as informed a decision as possible.
You don’t need us to tell you that the generational “leaps” are becoming less and less pronounced, even if you skip a few new releases.
Whether brands are holding certain functions back or other factors are at play is a topic rife among practically any industry observer right now. AI is playing a big role in the physical hardware you will buy now and for years to come.
In our eyes, there is only one key reason you should consider making the switch from a Pixel 9 to the Pixel 11, and that is if your phone is on its last legs or if you have the base 9 and want a telephoto lens. Those are the only two major reasons someone should consider the jump.
The Pixel 9 Pro and Pro XL are still fine phones. There seems to be no major or widespread issues that might cause people to be desperate to upgrade or switch away. It wasn’t the best phone on the market at launch, but, like any Pixel before, these devices tend to age better than others thanks to updates and enhancements courtesy of Google’s now-extensive support window.
If you’re even considering ditching a Pixel 9 Pro or Pro XL for the Pixel 11 lineup, think hard about what you’re actually getting. There isn’t anything on the software front that really warrants the substantial price increase. The new modem is good, but not a quantum leap. The camera improvements don’t provide exponential gains for photography or videography.
This is also true of most other pieces of tech right now. If your cell plan or contract is coming to an end imminently, maybe a cheap SIM plan could be a way to save cash at a time when smartphones are ballooning in price thanks to the constant march of AI development and the costs associated with the expansion.
The truth is that a two-generation upgrade cycle makes little sense today. You will simply get more bang for your buck by hanging on for another year. A battery replacement or repair would likely provide more value in most cases, given how little has truly changed over the past couple of years.
Follow Damien: Threads, Bluesky, Instagram
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-dark.png) 
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-light.png)
summary: Deciding whether to upgrade from a Google Pixel 9 to a Pixel 11 requires weighing minor iterative improvements like increased screen brightness, faster storage, and AI features against a largely unchanged design and identical core software experience. The article suggests that a two-generation upgrade cycle offers little value, advising users to hold onto their Pixel 9 devices unless their current phone is failing or they specifically want the base model's new telephoto lens.
key_points: The Pixel 9 and Pixel 11 feature nearly identical physical designs and core dimensions, though old cases will not fit due to a changed camera bar shape.
Pixel 11 displays offer a modest increase in maximum brightness, ranging from 10% on base models to 20% on Pro models.
The Pixel 11 introduces Gemini Intelligence and new camera features like customizable Camera Looks and a 120X zoom on Pro models, though RAM on the Pixel 11 Pro is lower than its predecessor.
Faster storage and a 256GB base model provide helpful long-term performance improvements.
The article concludes that a two-generation upgrade makes little financial sense, recommending users keep their Pixel 9 unless it is failing or they need a telephoto lens on a base model.

title: Nvidia’s new RTX Spark laptops launch in October with two different configs
author: Tom Warren
content:
All the rumors leading up to Nvidia’s announcement of its Arm-based RTX Spark chips over the summer mentioned two specific chips: the N1X and N1. While the N1 won’t be arriving this year, Nvidia says its N1X chip is arriving in RTX Spark laptops in two different configurations in October.
Nvidia’s new RTX Spark laptops launch in October with two different configs
Nvidia’s N1X laptop will ship in two different configurations for laptops and mini PCs.
![Screenshot_20260531_212701](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/05/Screenshot_20260531_212701.png?quality=90&strip=all&crop=1.6680227827502%2C0%2C96.6639544345%2C100&w=2400)
![Screenshot_20260531_212701](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/05/Screenshot_20260531_212701.png?quality=90&strip=all&crop=1.6680227827502%2C0%2C96.6639544345%2C100&w=2400)
You’ll be able to buy an RTX Spark N1X laptop with a configuration that I would call the mini PC chip. The top of the line N1X chip comes with a 6144-core Blackwell RTX GPU, paired with a 20-core Grace CPU and between 24GB and 128GB of unified memory. This particular chip will ship in both high-end laptops and miniature PCs like Microsoft’s Surface RTX Spark Dev Box.
![N1X configurations available in October.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/rtxsparknx1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
The more cut down N1X, or what I’d call the laptop chip, has a 5120-core Blackwell RTX GPU, combined with an 18-core Grace CPU and between 24GB and 32GB of unified memory. I’d expect most RTX Spark N1x laptops are going to use this chip, with devices launching from Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, or MSI in October.
We’re still waiting for Nvidia to share more on what the N1X is capable of for laptop gaming, but the company is vaguely promising 100fps 1440p gaming with ray-tracing and DLSS enabled for now. RTX Spark laptops are only a month away, so we’re also waiting to hear about exact availability and pricing from PC makers. With a RAMageddon crisis still looming large, I’m expecting to see N1X laptops priced at the very premium end of the market.
summary: Nvidia's Arm-based RTX Spark laptops featuring the N1X chip are scheduled to launch in October in two different configurations. The top-tier N1X configuration includes a 6144-core Blackwell RTX GPU and a 20-core Grace CPU, while the cut-down version features a 5120-core Blackwell RTX GPU and an 18-core Grace CPU. Devices utilizing these chips will be released by manufacturers such as Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI.
key_points: Nvidia's N1X chip will arrive in RTX Spark laptops and mini PCs in October.
The top-tier N1X configuration features a 6144-core Blackwell RTX GPU, a 20-core Grace CPU, and 24GB to 128GB of unified memory.
The cut-down N1X configuration includes a 5120-core Blackwell RTX GPU, an 18-core Grace CPU, and 24GB to 32GB of unified memory.
Laptops featuring the N1X will be launched by brands including Asus, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft, and MSI.

title: Belkin introduces its first longer-lasting semi-solid-state power banks
author: Andrew Liszewski
content:
Belkin is joining companies like BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens with the launch of its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology. The company claims the new accessories have been “engineered to last up to 3x longer than other power banks” with the addition of a “gel-like layer” alongside the liquid electrolyte typically found in lithium-ion batteries.
Belkin introduces its first longer-lasting semi-solid-state power banks
The company says its new power banks will last up to three times longer before they need to be replaced.
![belkin1](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkin1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.0099980003999178%2C100%2C99.9800039992&w=2400)
![belkin1](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkin1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0.0099980003999178%2C100%2C99.9800039992&w=2400)
Other advantages of what Belkin is calling its BoostSolid Cell technology include a reduced risk of overheating that could cause swelling or fires and consistent power delivery across a wider temperature range. They’re more expensive than power banks with comparable specs, but a longer functional lifespan should outweigh the premium pricing.
![A Belkin power bank attached to the back of a smartphone and plugged into a pair of wireless headphones.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkin2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
The UltraCharge Pro Slim Magnetic Power Bank 5K Qi2 15W with BoostSolid Cell is the smaller and cheaper option of Belkin’s two new power banks at $69.99. The company claims it’s 40 percent slimmer than other 5,000mAh power banks and is designed to magnetically hang on the back of compatible mobile devices and wirelessly deliver up to 15W of power. A USB-C charging port can also be used to power other devices at up to 22.5W, but charging two devices simultaneously drops the output to just 5W wirelessly and 12W with a USB-C cable.
![A Belkin power bank on a cooler connected to multiple devices.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/belkin3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)
The larger UltraCharge Pro Power Bank 10K 60W with BoostSolid Cell and Display offers twice the capacity with a 10,000mAh battery for an extra $20. The $89.99 power bank is also slimmer than competing options with similar capacities thanks to the increased energy density of its semi-solid-state battery tech. Power output maxes out at up to 60W when charging a single device over USB-C, but that drops when up to three devices are connected and charging using a pair of USB-C ports and a single USB-A port. And because putting screens on batteries is now en vogue, this one has a display showing charge level, power output, and the internal temperature.
summary: Belkin has launched its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology, marketed under the name BoostSolid Cell. These new accessories are engineered to last up to three times longer than standard power banks while offering a reduced risk of overheating and consistent power delivery across a wider temperature range. The lineup includes the 5K Qi2 15W model priced at $69.99 and the larger 10K 60W model with a display priced at $89.99.
key_points: Belkin's new power banks use semi-solid-state battery technology featuring a gel-like layer alongside liquid electrolyte.
The accessories are claimed to last up to three times longer than other power banks.
BoostSolid Cell technology reduces the risk of overheating and swelling while maintaining performance across a wider temperature range.
The UltraCharge Pro Slim Magnetic Power Bank 5K delivers up to 15W wirelessly and costs $69.99.
The UltraCharge Pro Power Bank 10K features a display and 60W max output, priced at $89.99.

title: Xiaomi 18 Fold with XRING O3 chip showcased at IFA 2026, we go eyes on
author: Michail
content:
Xiaomi is set to launch its 18 Fold next week, and we got to check it out at IFA 2026 ahead of its unveiling. Spoiler alert: the device was placed behind glass, so we could not actually get our hands on it, but we did get to marvel at its design, and the first thing that struck us was that bright red color.
It certainly pops and is a lot more vibrant in person than some of the earlier shots we saw online.
Moving on to the actual design, the 18 Fold adopts the short and wide “passport” look, which made headlines with the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, and we certainly dig this form factor.
Unlike the Z Fold8, the Xiaomi 18 Fold features more rounded corners, which seems like a great ergonomic approach by Xiaomi. We expect that it won’t dig into your palms when you use it for longer periods of time.
As a result of the rounded corners, the 5.38-inch cover screen gets a slightly weird look, with the left side featuring a more squared-off look while the corners on the right side are rounded.
The display bezels look slim enough, and we could not manage to make out the crease on the main 7.58-inch panel under most angles. Again, we did not get to touch the unit, so we’ll have to make our judgments once we actually get to hold one in hand. The main display features a punch-hole cutout in the top right corner for the selfie cam.
Speaking of cameras, you get a second front-facing shooter on the cover screen and three cameras on the back housed in a visor. We’re expecting to find a main, telephoto and ultrawide formation.
Xiaomi has already confirmed that the 18 Fold will be equipped with its in-house Xring O3 chipset, which shows promising performance. And that’s all we have to share at this moment in time.
For more details, we’ll check in after the official unveiling next week.
summary: Xiaomi showcased its upcoming 18 Fold smartphone behind glass at IFA 2026 ahead of next week's official launch. The foldable device features a vibrant bright red color, a short and wide "passport" form factor, and ergonomic rounded corners. It is equipped with the in-house Xring O3 chipset and includes a 5.38-inch cover screen alongside a 7.58-inch main display.
key_points: The Xiaomi 18 Fold was previewed behind glass at IFA 2026 before its launch next week.
It features a vibrant red color, a short and wide form factor, and rounded corners for better ergonomics.
The device includes a 5.38-inch cover display with an asymmetrical corner design and a 7.58-inch main panel.
Xiaomi has confirmed the device will be powered by its in-house Xring O3 chipset.

title: Ace Combat 8 reveals live service online multiplayer modes that include PvE, PvP, PvPvE battles, and a hangout space
author: Connor Makar
content:
Bandai Namco has revealed the live-service-like Ace Combat Online, a separate, companion selection of online modes coming with Ace Combat 8.
In a new video released to official Ace Combat social accounts, the developers revealed multiple game modes players will be able to engage with: either collaboratively or competitively.
Starting with the former, there are a selection of PvE modes coming to Ace Combat Online. Co-Op Assault places two teams of four against each other in a rush to earn points. By wiping out computer-controlled enemies and clearing objectives as a squad, players can duke it out for high scores.
Then there's Co-Op Warfare, where two teams of four face off in PvPvE. Each team has allied ground, air, and sea units that assist them in another score-based battle. The key difference is that here, the other team is present alongside you, trying to take you down. By taking out enemies, you build up a threat level which increases the points you gain, and the rewards the other team gets for taking you down.
There's also an airforce base, where player avatars can meet up and interact with each other. Not only is this a social space for team mates to linger between missions, you can hop on arcade machines to play retro Bandai Namco games like Pac-Man, and stand around a jukebox where older Ace Combat OSTs can be played. It's just like Top Gun.
There's another style of game mode too. Emergency missions are limited-time events that push players to engage in one of two special missions: Scramble or Emergency Sorties. In Scramble, your team of four has to take down an NPC-controlled rival squad. Emergency Sortie, on the other hand, places you and seven other pilots against a selection of set-piece fights from Ace Combat's history, in raid-style PvE engagements.
There are also limited-time 4v4 team battles and eight-player free-for-all missions present, which may come with various player restrictions to balance the battle somewhat.
By playing Ace Combat Online, you earn levels that in turn unlock more aircraft, special weapons, and aircraft parts that you can then take into further missions. You can also customise these planes with abilities and cosmetics, which are unlocked through playing with the aircraft.
Ace Combat Online comes with a free and paid Ace Pass, a battle pass where items can be unlocked and used in multiplayer matches. These seasons last just two months, though aircraft present in these passes will be available to buy after the season ends.
Speaking to Eurogamer at Gamescom, the decision to create a social hub for players to hang around in with Ace Combat Online was a response to a "fragmented" fanbase.
Manabu Shimomoto, producer for Ace Combat 8, said: "Ace Combat 7 was a success, and because of its success it created a lot of fans globally. However, due to the lack of opportunities for fans to get together, we received a lot of feedback that these fans wanted to meet up with others. To live up to that expectation, we decided to create this digital lobby.
"Ace Combat 7 sold seven-and-a-half-million copies, proving it was a successful game and it was played for a long time. Likewise, we want Ace Combat 8 to be played for a long time, and for it to be a long-term success, we wanted to create this opportunity."
summary: Bandai Namco has announced Ace Combat Online, a live-service companion to Ace Combat 8 featuring a variety of cooperative, competitive, and social multiplayer modes. The new offering includes PvE, PvP, and PvPvE battles, limited-time emergency missions, and a social airforce base hub. Players can earn levels, unlock aircraft and customization options, and progress through free and paid seasonal Ace Passes.
key_points: Ace Combat Online is a separate, companion multiplayer experience coming with Ace Combat 8.
Game modes include PvE, Co-Op Assault, Co-Op Warfare (PvPvE), and limited-time emergency missions like Scramble and Emergency Sorties.
A social airforce base hub allows player avatars to interact, play retro arcade games, and listen to classic soundtracks.
Players earn levels to unlock aircraft, weapons, parts, and cosmetics, alongside seasonal free and paid Ace Passes.
The social digital lobby was created in response to fan feedback following the success of Ace Combat 7 to help unite the global fanbase.

title: The Bentley Supersports: A stripped-out engineer's indulgence
author: Jonathan M Gitlin
content:
MONTEREY, Calif.—Last week, we brought news of the Bentley Torcal, a new electric vehicle that the luxury automaker has been cooking up at its HQ in Crewe, England. The company wants to attract new customers with its first battery EV, part of a plan to make sustainability as much a part of the brand’s character as its high-end fit and finish. W12 engines have given way to V8 plug-in hybrid power, and the new Continental GT is all the better for it.
But around the same time as Ars got its first experience of that new PHEV two-door on a rather wet Spanish racetrack, some of Bentley’s boffins were wondering what might happen if you also built one without the hybrid stuff.
Or all-wheel drive—something that has been a characteristic of every new road-going Bentley since the turn of the century. That would certainly cut the curb weight. So, too, would leaving out the rear seats. That sort of idea leads down a well-trodden path for some OEMs, and Porsche in particular is famous for making stripped-out road cars inspired by its race cars and making money from them, too.
![A pair of Bentley Supersports coupes descend through the Corkscrew at Laguna Seca](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Anthracite.Supersports-11.jpg) 
![](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/DragonRed.Supersports-2-1024x576.jpg) 
![](https://cdn.arstechnica.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Anthracite.Supersports-13-1024x683.jpg) 
Then again, Bentley still knows a thing or two about racing, most recently conquering the challenging and prestigious Bathurst 12 Hours race in 2020 with a GT3 version of the Continental GT3. And like that race car, its new Supersports settles for the relative simplicity of a 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 under the hood, powering just the rear wheels. There’s even more extreme aero than you expect to see on a road-legal car with a flying B badge, too.
summary: Bentley engineers developed the new Supersports as a stripped-out, rear-wheel-drive alternative to the brand's hybrid and all-wheel-drive vehicles. Inspired by race cars and Bentley's GT3 racing success, the model features a 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 engine, no rear seats, and extreme aerodynamics. This lightweight approach cuts curb weight significantly compared to standard modern Bentleys.
key_points: The Bentley Supersports was created as a stripped-out road car without hybrid systems or all-wheel drive.
It features a 4.0 L twin-turbo V8 engine powering only the rear wheels.
The design removes the rear seats and incorporates extreme aerodynamics inspired by race cars.
The vehicle draws on Bentley's racing heritage, including its 2020 Bathurst 12 Hours victory with the Continental GT3.

title: Mario Kart 8 Deluxe gets a free Switch 2 update adding an eight-player split-screen mode | VGC
author: Chris Scullion
content:
![Mario Kart 8 Deluxe gets a free Switch 2 update adding an eight-player split-screen mode](https://www.videogameschronicle.com/files/2026/09/mario-kart-8-320x180.jpg)
Nintendo has released a free Switch 2 update for Mario Kart 8 Deluxe.
The new Version 4.0.0 update is available for all Switch users, but the majority of the changes are exclusively available to those playing on Switch 2.
The most notable addition in the new update is local support for 5-8 players on one display on Switch 2, as opposed to the 1-4 player support on Switch.
This means, assuming there are enough players and enough controllers, an eight-player split-screen race is now possible due to the Switch 2’s increased power and resolution.
While players can use original Nintendo Switch controllers (such as Switch Joy-Cons and Pro Controllers) for these multiplayer races, only seven last-gen controllers can connect to the Switch 2, meaning if an 8-player race is selected at least one player needs to have a Switch 2 Pro Controller or Joy-Con 2.
As well as this, CameraPlay support has been added, meaning players who own the Switch 2 camera or any other compatible USB camera can now use it to show their face during 2-4 player local multiplayer and Online Play modes.
For security reasons, players using their camera online can only do so with their friends in GameChat, rather than with random players online.
![Mario Kart 8 Deluxe gets a free Switch 2 update adding an eight-player split-screen mode](https://www.videogameschronicle.com/files/2026/09/mario-kart-8-deluxe-80x45.jpg)
The update also increases the game’s resolution on Switch 2, and shortens the loading time before races and battles begin.
Players on the original Switch aren’t entirely unaffected by the Version 4.0.0 update. The game has been made slightly faster, with player speed increased during races “by the equivalent of one coin”.
A new ’96 Races’ option has also been added to the VS Race setting for players with the Booster Course Pass, meaning they can take part in a marathon GP consisting of all 96 races in order. Before the update, only a maximum of 48 races could be played in a row in VS Race.

title: Google announces September Android drop, here are all the new features
author: Vlad
content:
Today Google has announced its September Android drop, which incorporates five new features coming to Android devices left and right.
So let's dive right in. You will "soon" be able to ask Gemini to remember where you put important items and it will save their location in Google's Find Hub so you can easily find them later. This is intended for things you don't put a tracker tag on, like your passport or a spare key. Just tell Gemini where the item is - or maybe add an optional photo. When you need to find it, either ask Gemini for its location or check the remembered items tab in Find Hub. This will be available on Android 16 and later in countries where Gemini and Find Hub are available.
Motion Assist helps reduce motion sickness by using a bubble overlay on the screen, which moves with the vehicle you're in. Google says it's "designed to bridge the gap between what your eyes see and the movement of your ride". You can set this to turn on automatically, add it to Quick Settings, and customize the shape, color, and opacity of the bubbles. This is only coming to devices running Android 17.
Guided vision can help read fine print on a food label, order from a menu in a low-lit restaurant, or identify household objects, and all you need to do is share your camera in Gemini Live. If the camera isn't lined up, voice feedback will guide you to reframe it, pan across a space, or center an object so you get the answers you want. You can add Guided vision to your Accessibility shortcuts or enable it directly from the TalkBack menu or the Gemini app's settings. This is coming soon to devices running Android 9 and later in countries where Gemini is available.
You can now share and update Google Keep grocery lists or notes right inside your chat in Google Messages, and all of the participants can view, edit, and add ideas to your note or list. You just need to hit the "+" icon in Google Messages. The rollout of this feature has already started in Google Messages.
Finally, and speaking of Google Messages, you can customize each chat with a different background and color theme. You can pick a wallpaper or a photo and the bubble colors will automatically match, but you can also change them if you want to. This is available now in Google Messages.
summary: Google has announced its September Android feature drop, introducing five new capabilities for Android devices. The updates include Gemini integration with Find Hub for remembering item locations, a Motion Assist tool for reducing motion sickness, and Guided vision for accessibility assistance using Gemini Live. Additionally, users can now share Google Keep lists and customize individual chat backgrounds and color themes directly within Google Messages.
key_points: Gemini will soon allow users to save and find item locations using Google's Find Hub.
Motion Assist uses a customizable screen bubble overlay to help reduce motion sickness on vehicles.
Guided vision uses Gemini Live and camera sharing with voice feedback to assist users with reading and identifying objects.
Google Keep notes and grocery lists can now be shared and edited directly inside Google Messages chats.
Google Messages now allows users to customize individual chats with unique wallpapers, photos, and matching color themes.

title: Xbox Down For You? Microsoft Acknowledges 'Major Outage' as Sign-In Issues Hit PC and Console [UPDATED]
author: Tom Phillips
content:
UPDATE: Microsoft has said it's now addressed the issues that caused an Xbox services outage earlier today, bringing players back online.
"Great news, everyone! Engineering has confirmed mitigation," reads a new post on the Xbox Support social media account. "Signing in or creating an account should be back to normal now. We appreciate the heads-up — keep them coming if anything else pops up."
All in all, the issue appears to have been resolved within six hours.
ORIGINAL STORY: Microsoft has acknowledged a "major outage," with account issues across PC, Xbox Series X/S, and other devices.
If you're struggling to log into your Xbox account in order to play games, you're not alone. Numerous reports of issues have popped up this morning, and Microsoft itself has now acknowledged the problem.
Describing the incident as a major outage, the Xbox Support page for the issue explains that impacted users "may not be able to sign-in to your Xbox profile, may be disconnected while signed in, or have other related problems."
Meanwhile, "features that require sign-in like most games, apps and social activity won't be available." Impacted platforms include Xbox Series X/S, Xbox One, Xbox 360, Xbox on Windows, Android, iPhone, Cloud and web services.
Microsoft initially acknowledged the issue at 5.:09am ET today, and is still working on the issue some four hours later. As yet, there's no word on the reason behind the outage.
We are aware that some users are encountering errors when attempting to sign in or create an account. Thank you for your patience while we investigate this issue. We'll update as soon as we have more — keep an eye on https://t.co/MGxnmqdcis.

The outage impacted various platforms, including Xbox consoles, Windows PC, mobile devices, and cloud services.
Users were unable to sign in, create accounts, or access games, apps, and social features.
The entire incident was resolved within approximately six hours of the initial report.

title: Acer’s new MacBook Air rival is nearly a pound lighter than Apple’s laptop
author: Antonio G Di Benedetto
content: Acer is announcing a new laptop poised to rival the MacBook Air’s thinness and lightness — and in the process, it cops another laptop’s name. The Acer Swift Blade 14 (not to be confused with the Razer Blade 14) is a productivity machine weighing just 1.76 pounds / 799g and measuring as little as 0.51 inches / 12.95mm thin. That’s around 1.7mm thicker than Apple’s svelte 13-inch MacBook Air, but Acer’s Blade is nearly a pound lighter. Its featherweight stature is partly due to Acer using carbon fiber in the laptop’s top lid and bottom plate. Acer’s new MacBook Air rival is nearly a pound lighter than Apple’s laptop The half-inch thin laptop is joined by a new, much larger Swift Air 16 — both with Intel Wildcat Lake. ![Acer Swift Blade 14 SFB14-53CF Lifestyle 02](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Blade-14-SFB14-53CF-Lifestyle-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=3.8%2C0%2C92.4%2C100&w=2400) ![Acer Swift Blade 14 SFB14-53CF Lifestyle 02](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Blade-14-SFB14-53CF-Lifestyle-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=3.8%2C0%2C92.4%2C100&w=2400) Inside the Swift Blade will be a range of Intel Wildcat Lake processors, from the lowly five-core Core 3 304 that I tested in the Chuwi UniBook to the six-core Intel Core 7 350. And regardless of which exact chip is inside, the Acer will come with 12GB of RAM. So it’s not likely that the Acer will go toe-to-toe with the MacBook Air’s M5 chip in terms of raw performance, but it could make a compelling case for someone who prefers their laptop to be about as light as they come. ![Pretty thin for marshmallows.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Blade-14-SFB14-53CF-open-closed-angles.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![Two USB-C ports on the left.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Blade-14-SFB14-53CF-closed-lid-colors.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![One more USB-C, a USB-A, and a 3.5mm audio jack on the right.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Blade-14-SFB14-53CF-front-back.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) The Swift Blade will come with a basic 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz IPS LCD screen with just 300 nits of brightness, but there will be a couple of OLED options as well (up to 2880 x 1800 / 90Hz and 400 nits). The OLED versions make the chassis ever-so-slightly thicker. And the laptop will have three USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 ports (one of which will be data-only) and a 3.5mm audio jack. Acer isn’t sharing pricing for any configurations of the Swift Blade 14 until closer to its December launch. It’s the same story for the other Swift laptop Acer is announcing today: the Swift Air 16. This is a larger version of the Swift Air 14 announced at Computex. Despite being named Air, the Swift Air 14 was aimed squarely at the MacBook Neo — especially with its price of $699. While we don’t know yet what the Swift Air 16 will cost, we know it’ll offer similar Intel Wildcat Lake chips, Thunderbolt 4 ports, options for OLED screens, up to 16GB of RAM, and up to 512GB of NVMe storage. It’s not as light as the Swift Blade 14, but at 0.53 inches / 13.5mm thick and 3.31 pounds / 1.5kg, the Swift Air 16 sounds pretty light and thin for a 16-inch. It’s due to arrive in North America in Q1 2027 and other regions this December. ![The Acer Swift Air 16.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Air-16-SFA16-I31T-open-closed-colors.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400) ![It will come in blue (pictured), green, and sandstone gold (which looks like rose gold in renders).](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/Acer-Swift-Air-16-SFA16-I31T-front-back-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=2400)
summary: Acer has announced the Swift Blade 14, a productivity laptop designed to rival the MacBook Air by weighing just 1.76 pounds, making it nearly a pound lighter than Apple's laptop. The featherweight device achieves its low weight using carbon fiber in the top lid and bottom plate and is powered by Intel Wildcat Lake processors. Acer also introduced the larger Swift Air 16, featuring similar Intel processors and options for OLED screens.
key_points: The Acer Swift Blade 14 weighs 1.76 pounds and measures 0.51 inches thin.
Carbon fiber is used in the Swift Blade 14's top lid and bottom plate to reduce weight.
The Swift Blade 14 features Intel Wildcat Lake processors and 12GB of RAM.
Acer also announced the Swift Air 16, a larger 16-inch laptop with Intel Wildcat Lake chips and up to 16GB of RAM.

title: First Drive: The Bentley Continental Supersports Has Hit the Gym
author: Matt Farah
content:
Enthusiasts spend a lot of time lamenting car bloat, the general trend for cars to get bigger, heavier, and more high-tech, then becoming more powerful to deal with that heft, then requiring even more heft to deliver and control the increased power. Curb weights go up, engagement levels go down. We complain about it almost across the board, from Corvettes to Super Duty pickup trucks.
I complain about it more than most. But not across the board. Because one brand consistently gets a pass: Bentley. As far as I’m concerned, for the Continental GT and its siblings, mass is a feature, not a bug. Everything on these cars is thicker, denser, more reinforced, and more layered in order to better isolate the people on the inside from the real world outside.
Yes, despite this, I have also driven Bentleys on racetracks. You do sometimes see them there even if I’m not in the vicinity, although generally parked in the paddock rather than muscling their way around the circuit itself. But you would likely be shocked at how well a GT Speed does a fourth-gear slide, or how nicely the Continental V8 S with optional carbon-ceramic brakes held up to a 30-minute track session at the demanding Sonoma Raceway.
But although a Continental GT, a GT S, or a GT Speed will hold up well to track work, they have not been optimized for the task. So what about a Bentley that has been? Could it be turned into a real, connected driver’s car of the sort you really would take to a track day or buy as a weekend canyon car? Could it be stripped down and pared back and made, well, almost lightweight?
My first chance to drive the new Continental Supersports came on track at Laguna Seca. This wasn’t a comprehensive test; I was limited to six laps on track with the active safety systems all fully enabled and with a chaperone in the passenger seat. There would be no road driving. It was a short go, but a promising one.
The Supersports isn’t just the lightest Continental GT ever, it is the lightest Bentley road car in 85 years. It really has been nearly a century since a Bentley had a curb weight beginning with a three. Although not yet officially certified, the company says the Supersports is on track to come in at 1995 kilograms, or 4398 pounds, just under two metric tons. Did you just chuckle a bit because nearly 4400 pounds is objectively not light? Fair enough, but consider that the current Continental GT Speed is over a thousand pounds heavier than the Supersports. That is an impressive commitment to shedding mass, with the biggest reductions coming through a switch to rear-wheel drive and losing the regular Conti’s plug-in hybrid system.
The Supersports looks different, with the deep chin splitter, wing, and rocker panels giving off Mustang Dark Horse vibes. That’s not a bad thing, and the carbon body panels and aero components don’t just reduce weight, they also help to rebalance the aerodynamics that have changed as the center of mass has been altered by the loss of the driven front axle, high-voltage battery pack, and rear seats. Bentley claims an increase in downforce by up to 660 pounds over the GT Speed. The 22-inch forged alloy wheels also reduce unsprung weight and bring in an unlikely Porsche crossover—they are made by Manthey, which has engineered them for both lightness and strength.
The front seats are lower than those of other Contis, and they have been stripped of massage functions but have grown deeper side bolsters and shoulder support. The rest of the interior, insanely two-tone in the car I drove, is familiar from the other members of the Continental GT clan, with carbon-fiber-weave dash inserts. Round metal air vents with fantastically fluid-feeling plungers have survived, but the James Bond–esque rotating center display screen has been sacrificed as part of the weight-saving strategy.
Working without a plug-in hybrid system, the Supersports is also the least powerful current-generation Continental, despite its 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 making 657 hp and 590 lb-ft in its own right—with all that power going to the rear wheels only. Zero to 60 is . . . not the point. But it’s also somewhere under four seconds, depending on traction. Which, on track, is enhanced with the Pirelli P Zero Trofeo RS tires I experienced the car on.
It also stops. With 17.3-inch diameter carbon-ceramic discs up front, the largest fitted to any road car, with 10-piston calipers the Supersports has huge braking power. The 16.1-inch rear discs with four-pot calipers are only slightly less wild. Air suspension is still present, with twin-valve dampers for Tour and Sport drive modes. Like the regular Conti GT, a 48-volt active anti-roll system keeps the body in check, and rear-steering and an electronically controlled rear differential round out the big-ticket handling items.
With so little time in the driver’s seat, I got to harvesting impressions as soon as I hit the track. Right away, the Supersports’ body felt strapped down tighter to its wheel hubs. The ripples of Laguna’s curbs came through in the wheel, not violently, but enough to properly transmit the texture of the surface. The brakes, too, impressed, at least over what was a short stint. Hard, repeated stops on track didn’t illicit much sense of fade.
Boy, did it want to slide. Just over 650 horses is a lot to send to the rear wheels of a front-engined car, and even with the traction control engaged the Supersports would step its back end out when braking into a corner. This was good, and I soon learned that it was consistent with its level of oversteer and that getting sideways on entry is the proper way to get the car turned. I just had to modulate the throttle and keep the angle held for the remainder of the corner.
But, sadly, the traction control was a real buzzkill, denying me the chance to further influence the Supersports’ line with more power. Unlike Aston Martin, Ferrari, or McLaren’s more adept traction management systems, Bentley’s cut the throttle entirely, snapping mild oversteer back into place well before anything more exciting could develop. I know that the modern all-wheel-drive Bentleys are much more fun with the systems fully de-energized; I imagine it will be the same with the Supersports.
But let’s talk about the way the new car handled Laguna Seca’s corners six through 10, where you definitely want poise over sideways thrills: a fast, high-g kink, the Corkscrew, and one of the scariest downhill off-camber corners in motorsports. Here the Supersports got big points, loading up the front right tire beautifully with just a smidge of push across six, brutish enough to take the “Zanardi line” through the Corkscrew. And while I had to stab the brakes before turning into Turn 9, the back end didn’t step out—that behavior is reserved for the slower, tighter turns you want it for.
The one real weak point to driving any modern Continental on track is when manually shifting. The software controlling the dual-clutch gearbox insists on far more margin than is strictly necessary to give a downshift; it won’t allow one that will put the engine toward the top of its rev range, even if that would be well short of the limiter. I was hoping the Supersports would get a unique shift program to change this, but sadly no. So my one real dynamic complaint remains: Don’t tug the down paddle until the revs fall to 3500 rpm or so. In the car, or standing trackside, the Supersports’ V-8 sounds tremendous, with a guttural, baritone sound. But the noise doesn’t carry very far—stand a hundred yards farther away and you barely hear a thing.
The Supersports is a limited edition sitting at the top of the Continental GT range, and it is priced accordingly. The base is $486,000, plus destination, delivery, and taxes. The wild, Ombre paint; the split-color cockpit; and plenty of smaller enhancements all cost extra, a lot more through Bentley’s Mulliner customization department. Expect the final number for a car specified like this one to start with a five, maybe even a six. That’s a big enough number that buyers will be cross-shopping exotic material, maybe even investment-grade cars. The Supersports is not a rational purchase, but Bentley says the entire run of 500 is already accounted for. 
Which is further proof of the strange way the most luxurious end of the luxury market operates. It costs a ton of money to put all the performance, features, and tech into a Bentley Continental GT. And it costs even more to take them back out.
summary: The author tested the new Bentley Continental Supersports during a brief track session at Laguna Seca. This limited-edition model is significantly lighter than the standard Continental GT due to the removal of the plug-in hybrid system, front-wheel-drive components, rear seats, and other features. Powered by a 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 producing 657 horsepower sent exclusively to the rear wheels, the Supersports offers improved track handling and agility despite weighing nearly 4,400 pounds. Although the base price starts at $486,000, Bentley reports that the entire run of 500 units is already spoken for.
key_points: The Continental Supersports is the lightest Bentley road car in 85 years, weighing an estimated 4,398 pounds—over a thousand pounds lighter than the current GT Speed.
Weight savings were achieved by switching to rear-wheel drive, removing the plug-in hybrid system and rear seats, and adopting carbon body panels and Manthey-engineered 22-inch forged alloy wheels.
It features a 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8 engine that delivers 657 horsepower and 590 lb-ft of torque to the rear wheels.
The vehicle is equipped with massive 17.3-inch front carbon-ceramic brakes and features aggressive aerodynamics that increase downforce significantly.
Priced starting at $486,000, all 500 units of the limited-edition Supersports are already accounted for.

title: Sonos Ace Ultra feature all-new drivers, updated ANC, and a "direct connection" to the current Sonos ecosystem
author: Kashfia Kabir
content:
![Sonos Ace Ultra headphones](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/hHiZiQqUTYHhVHL9G3i76c.jpg) 
The Sonos Ace Ultra wireless headphones have landed, and it looks like good news throughout, with Sonos promising a "direct connection to the Sonos system."
Positioned above the three-star Ace – the brand's first headphones released in 2024 – the new step-up Ace Ultra have been designed from the ground up to deliver the improvements to sound, noise-cancelling and wider compatibility with the Sonos ecosystem that were missing from Sonos' debut over-ears.
At the heart of the Ace Ultra is the "Headphone Engine 2", a next-gen wi-fi hardware and software system that lets you link the headphones directly to your existing Sonos system. It's the feature that we (and Sonos customers) have wanted all along, allowing you to swap audio from any Sonos wireless speaker or soundbar to the Ace Ultra headphones at the press of a button (or via the app), and back again.
Listening to music on the Ace Ultra from your laptop or smartphone is still done via Bluetooth rather than wi-fi, but this is a marked improvement over the original Sonos Ace, where you could only 'swap' audio from select Sonos soundbars.
With the Ace Ultra, this 'headphone linking' feature will work with any current Sonos soundbar and wireless speaker under the Sonos 27 ecosystem, including the Arc Ultra, Ray, Beam (Gen 2), new Beam Ultra, Sonos Five, Era 100, Era 300, Move 2, Play and Roam 2.
 ![Sonos Ace Ultra headphones](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/yzTKjLWXZM7XG9nL56VUwb.jpg) 
The Ace Ultra feature all-new Sonos-designed 40mm drivers, and the sound is tuned with input from the Sonos Soundboard, which features leading figures in music and film (including Grammy winners) to deliver a sound "that stays true to the artist's intent."
Active noise cancellation has been given a boost, with the Ace Ultra promising to be twice as effective in this regard. The Ace Ultra house 10 mics (up from eight on the original Ace), with an adaptive ANC system that continuously monitors your surroundings to deliver the best ANC experience.
The latest hi-fi, home cinema and tech news, reviews, buying advice and deals, direct to your inbox.
An Adaptive EQ also tunes the ANC to adjust to any imperfections in the acoustic seal around the earcups, such as gaps in the fit for those wearing glasses.
An Aware mode, which lets outside sounds in, also returns, as does support for headtracking with Dolby Atmos content.
Battery is up to 35 hours (up from 30 hours from the original Ace) with ANC activated, and you can get three hours from a fast-charge of three minutes. The higher-quality aptX Lossless codec is supported, while native support for 16-bit/48kHz resolution is once again supported via a wired USB-C connection.
 ![Sonos Ace Ultra wireless headphones](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ycbivHgiod6aTz4nZDk2Vh.jpg) 
The general design of the Sonos Ace Ultra remains the same as before, with soft foam cushions to provide maximum comfort, and physical buttons that include a multi-function button/slider (called the 'control key') through which you can adjust volume, change noise modes and playback, and send music to and from your connected Sonos speakers via the 'headphone linking' feature.
There are three-band and eight-band EQ settings in the app to further customise the sound to your tastes, whereas TrueCinema technology tunes the headphones' sound according to your room's acoustics when connected to a compatible Sonos soundbar.
The Sonos Ace Ultra headphones will cost £399 / $449 and be available globally from 29th September, with pre-orders starting from today, 1st September. The headphones will be available in four finishes: new sand and agave colours, as well as the standard black and white options.
Interestingly, the established Sonos Ace will continue to be available. The Ace are currently priced at £299 / $299 / AU$449, which is a considerable drop from their launch price of £449 / $449 / AU$699. Those in the UK will also get a bonus saving, as the new Ace Ultra will launch for £50 less than the inaugural Ace did.
We have high hopes for the new Sonos Ace Ultra headphones, which seem to address many of the issues we had with the original Ace – such as incomplete features, buggy connections, "average" sound, and ANC quality that didn't compete with strong rivals.
Let's see if they give the current Sony, Bose and Sennheiser class leaders a run for their money.

Read our original Sonos Ace review
And our five-star Sony WH-1000XM6 review
Best wireless headphones 2026: reviewed and rated by our in-house experts
![Kashfia Kabir](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/W5LyjQLnpURpF8S2awFAXm.jpg)
Kashfia is the Hi-Fi and Audio Editor of What Hi-Fi? and first joined the brand 14 years ago. During her time in the consumer tech industry, she has reviewed hundreds of products (including speakers, amplifiers, turntables and headphones), been to countless trade shows across the world and fallen in love with hi-fi kit much bigger than her. In her spare time, Kash can be found tending to an ever-growing houseplant collection and shooing her cat away from spinning records.

summary: Sonos has announced the Ace Ultra wireless headphones, positioned above the original Ace model with major upgrades to sound quality, active noise cancellation, and ecosystem compatibility. Powered by the new Headphone Engine 2, the headphones feature direct wi-fi linking to any current Sonos soundbar and wireless speaker. Priced at £399 / $449, they launch globally on September 29 with pre-orders beginning September 1.
key_points: The Headphone Engine 2 enables direct wi-fi connection to swap audio between any current Sonos soundbar or wireless speaker and the headphones.
Features all-new 40mm drivers tuned with input from the Sonos Soundboard.
Active noise cancellation is twice as effective, utilizing 10 microphones and an adaptive system.
Battery life offers up to 35 hours with ANC activated, alongside a fast-charge option providing three hours of use from a three-minute charge.
Available in four color finishes (sand, agave, black, and white) for £399 / $449, releasing globally on September 29.

title: Sonos' new Beam soundbar is finally here with a big Dolby Atmos upgrade – but there’s still something missing
author: Robyn Quick
content:
![Sonos Beam Ultra on a black table, with someone touching the end with their hand.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/k8Vpd8RJRsjpbDaCkQ8Qrb.jpg) 
Sonos has finally launched a new version of its Award-winning Sonos Beam (Gen 2) soundbar.
The new Beam Ultra was unveiled at a pre-launch press event today and sits in the same family as the more premium Arc Ultra, which came out in 2024.
The “mid-size soundbar” boasts a 7.1.2-channel configuration. This includes two up-firing drivers.
The up-firing drivers are a key upgrade over the older Beam Gen 2, which didn't feature them.
Despite the upgrade, there is still no DTS:X support. The omission isn't a huge surprise, as none of the company’s soundbars features it, but it is a bit of a shame for those wanting comprehensive surround sound options.
When asked whether Sonos would add DTS:X in the future, Senior Director of Product Development at Sonos, Brandon Holley told us: "The door isn't closed for us, but just in terms of delivering the value that we think our customers are specifically asking for, that's what Beam Ultra has today."
The Beam Ultra also features a redesigned centre channel and four levels of AI Speech Enhancement to help it deliver clearer dialogue.
The latest hi-fi, home cinema and tech news, reviews, buying advice and deals, direct to your inbox.
There’s also a Night Sound setting if you don’t want to disturb the neighbours, which should compress the bar's dynamic range. Once again, the firm's Trueplay calibration is on hand to fine-tune the sound to your space.
You can also link the Beam Ultra with other Sonos products to create a multi-room listening experience, including the newly announced Sonos Ace Ultra over-ear headphones.
 ![Sonos Beam Ultra wall mounted on a white background](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PhcC3PRNxDgpwXnf58yrqV.jpg) 
Holley added that the firm has worked to ensure the Beam Ultra delivers better audio with music, telling us: "We treat music as important as we do home theatre performance, and so we want it to sound great musically as a soundbar as well."
That's something we found to be true with Sonos' previous models, so we are hopeful it will be the same with the new addition.
The Beam Ultra will be available in two finishes (black and white) and you can mount the bar to your wall or simply place it in front of your TV. We don't have its full dimensions yet, but Holley told us that the Beam Ultra has been intentionally designed not to block the TV screen, even if it is sitting on the surface.
So, how much will the new soundbar set you back? In the UK, the Beam Ultra will launch at £699 (around $946 / AU$1320). That means it sits between the Sonos Arc Ultra and the Sonos Beam Gen 2, which launched at £999 / $999 / AU$1799 and £449 / $449 / AU$649, respectively. The base Beam Gen 2 will remain on sale, sitting below the Ultra in Sonos' range.
We haven't managed to get the Beam Ultra into our test room yet, but we should have a chance to get up close with it very soon at the IFA trade show in Berlin. Watch this space.

summary: Sonos has announced the new Beam Ultra mid-size soundbar, featuring a 7.1.2-channel configuration with two up-firing drivers for an upgraded Dolby Atmos experience. The device also includes a redesigned centre channel, AI Speech Enhancement, and music performance improvements, though it still lacks DTS:X support. Priced at £699, it sits between the Arc Ultra and the base Beam Gen 2, which will remain on sale.
